No, that's not right, and it matters for your design. A language model doesn't remember earlier conversations on its own.

The model has no memory between requests. Each time your assistant calls it, the model sees only the text you send in that call: the instructions, the conversation so far, any tool results. When the call ends, nothing is kept inside the model. A chatbot that seems to remember is an app that resends the earlier messages each time.

Here is an example. Last week a student told your assistant, "I've done the laser cutter safety training." This week they open a new session and ask, "Can I book the laser cutter?" The model has never seen last week's message, so it can't know about the training. It will either ask again or guess.

This is why your mission has a decision about "what it saves between sessions." Your app has to do the remembering:

1. Save the facts that matter, such as training status, in a database or file keyed by student.
2. At the start of the next session, load that record and put it into the model's context.

The model then "remembers" only because you put the facts in front of it. This also affects your budget, because everything you load costs tokens on every request. That is the reason to save short facts and not whole transcripts.

Quick check: if a student says "use the same time as last week," what would your assistant need to fetch before the model could answer?

I can turn this into a short lesson on context and memory, which is next in your plan. Want one?
